strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: transferring in-context learning capabilities to smaller models. Aligning teacher and student preferences over demonstration subsets is a coherent, well-motivated extension of output distillation.

Table 2 reports improvements over every evaluated baseline across all five benchmarks. BiAlign achieves a 30.2 average versus 29.2 for Output-Align and 29.4 for fine-tuning, providing encouraging initial evidence of transfer beyond the source tasks.

The objectives, diagrams, and pseudocode make the main approach understandable. Public models and datasets, several training hyperparameters, and experiments varying subset count and demonstration count provide a useful foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The reliability of the gains remains unresolved. No training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or paired significance analyses are reported, despite improvements as small as 0.2 percentage points over Output-Align on MMLU. The HumanEval increase from 14.6 to 15.2 corresponds to only one additional solved problem out of 164. These results support a promising trend but do not yet substantiate robust superiority.

The experiments insufficiently isolate the proposed ranking mechanism. Output-Align is a relevant component baseline, but BiAlign additionally processes multiple sampled subset contexts. A baseline applying output distillation or supervised training to those same contexts, with comparable computation, is needed to distinguish ranking benefits from additional context exposure. Comparisons with simpler ranking objectives and measurements of teacher–student ranking agreement would strengthen the central claim.

The evaluation protocol contains an unresolved numerical inconsistency. Under the stated greedy evaluation on 164 HumanEval problems, the FT score of 14.2 and C-Pretrain score of 13.2 cannot be rounded percentages of integer success counts. Averaging across runs could explain this, but no aggregation procedure is described. The evaluated splits, metrics, and run counts need explicit clarification.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful high-level description. The manuscript supplies no implementation link or exact constructed training set and omits consequential details such as training prompt templates, optimizer settings, and sequence truncation. Equation 3 also divides by the student score range without specifying stabilization when that range vanishes or handling of teacher-score ties. The appendix contains no additional information.

The broader conclusions exceed the demonstrated scope. Only one teacher–student pair, Llama 2-13B to 7B, is evaluated, and additional training costs are unreported. Higher few-shot accuracy alone does not establish stronger use of demonstrations rather than improved general task performance; zero-shot and varying-shot comparisons on the same tasks would clarify this distinction. These limitations constrain broader merits, while the experimental-control and reporting gaps above require revision before a positive Findings recommendation.
